source_title: Man buys two paintings for $60, discovers they're worth $1.072m; sellers lose
source_excerpt: In 1996, Carl Rice attended an Arizona estate sale, spotted two framed oil paintings priced at $30 each, and paid the $60 asking price without expecting anything extraordinary. He liked the subject matter of one painting and the frame of the other, but assumed that paintings sold so cheaply by a professionally managed estate could not be original works by a major artist. That assumption proved spectacularly wrong. The paintings were later authenticated as works by Martin Johnson Heade, a celebrated 19th century American painter, and sold at Christieâs for a combined $1.072 million. The story did not end with the auction. Martha Nelsonâs estate, whose personal representatives had organised the sale, later sued Rice and his wife Anne in an effort to undo the transaction. The estate argued that both sides had made a mutual mistake about the paintingsâ value and that enforcing the sale would be unconscionable. But the Arizona Court of Appeals disagreed, affirming the lower courtâs decision and leaving the Rices with the proceeds. The case remains a striking example of how estate sales can hide extraordinary value, and of how the law treats a bargain made in good faith.A $60 purchase at an estate saleAccording to Justia U.S. Law, After Martha Nelson died in February 1996, her estateâs personal representatives, Kenneth Newman and Edward Franz, hired Judith McKenzie-Larson to appraise the personal property before an estate sale. McKenzie-Larson told them that she did not appraise fine art and that they would need another appraiser if any fine art were found. She did not report finding any, and relying on her appraisal, the representatives priced and sold the estateâs belongings.Carl Rice responded to a newspaper advertisement and attended the public sale. He paid the estateâs asking price of $60 for two oil paintings. Although he had bought and sold some art before, he was not a trained or sophisticated collector. Court records note that he had never made more than $55 on a single piece and had previously purchased works that turned out to be frauds, forgeries, or pieces by lesser known artists.Rice later said he assumed the paintings were not originals because of the low price and because the estate appeared to be professionally managed. Still, something about them caught his attention. He was drawn to the subject of one painting and the frame of the other, and after bringing them home he compared the signatures with examples in a book of artistsâ signatures. The signatures appeared similar to that of Martin Johnson Heade.The discovery that changed everythingFollowing their usual practice, the Rices sent photographs of the paintings to Christieâs in New York to see whether they might be Headeâs work. Christieâs authenticated both paintings, Magnolia Blossoms on Blue Velvet and Cherokee Roses, as genuine works by Heade. The auction house then offered to sell them on consignment. Christieâs later sold the paintings at auction for $1,072,000. After deducting the buyerâs premium and commission, the Rices received $911,780. They paid $337,000 in income taxes on the profit in 1997, bought a home, created a family trust, and used part of the money for living expenses. What had begun as an ordinary $60 estate sale purchase had become a life changing windfall, as per Justia U.S. Law.Magnolia Blossoms on Blue Velvet is an oil on canvas measuring 15 by 24 inches and signed âM.J. Headeâ in the lower right. Christieâs records trace its ownership through the Sleeth family of Belleville, New Jersey and Tucson, Arizona, before it passed by bequest to Robert G. Nelson and then to Martha Campbell Nelson, whose estate sold it. The auction house describes it as one of Headeâs extraordinary floral still lifes, painted around 1890 after the artist moved to St. Augustine, Florida.The estate went to courtThe estateâs representatives learned of the sale in February 1997. They first sued McKenzie-Larson, believing she was responsible for the loss, but settled that case after discovering she had no assets with which to pay damages. In late January 1998, the estate sued the Rices, seeking to rescind or reform the sale on the grounds of mutual mistake and unconscionability.The estate argued that neither party knew the transaction involved fine art. It claimed both sides believed they were dealing with relatively valueless wall decorations rather than valuable paintings. The Rices responded that the estate bore the risk of any mistake, that the doctrine of laches prevented reformation of the contract, and that unconscionability was not a proper basis for rescinding the sale.The trial court found that although both parties had been mistaken about the paintingsâ value, the estate bore the risk of that mistake. It also found that the contract was not unconscionable because the parties had not negotiated the price. The estate had set the price, and Rice had simply paid it. The court denied the estateâs motion for summary judgment, granted the Ricesâ cross motion, and later denied the estateâs request for a new trial.Why the Rices kept the windfallOn appeal, the estate argued that the mutual mistake should allow the sale to be rescinded. The Arizona Court of Appeals explained that a party seeking rescission must prove the claim by clear and convincing evidence. More importantly, the party asking for relief cannot bear the risk of the mistake. The court found that the estate did bear that risk.The personal representatives had hired two appraisers for the estateâs collection of Indian art and artifacts, but McKenzie-Larson had specifically said she did not appraise fine art. Newman testified that he was not concerned about her lack of expertise because he believed the estate contained nothing of significant value besides the house and the Indian art collection. Despite knowing that framed art existed beyond the Indian pieces, the representatives relied on someone admittedly unqualified to determine whether fine art was present.The appellate court characterized this as conscious ignorance. By choosing not to hire a qualified fine art appraiser, the estate knowingly proceeded despite its limited knowledge. The court also noted that the estate had ample opportunity to discover what it was selling and failed to do so, acting only after learning the paintingsâ worth through the Ricesâ own efforts. In the courtâs view, the estate was a victim of its own folly, making it reasonable to allocate the burden of the mistake to the estate.A lesson in estate sale fortunesThe court also rejected the estateâs unconscionability argument. While the outcome may have seemed unfair in hindsight, the judges found that the terms of the contract were not. There had been no negotiation, the estate dictated the price for each painting, and Rice paid exactly what was asked. The court said it would be overly paternalistic to relieve a party from the consequences of what was, at worst, a bad bargain.The decision was affirmed in 2000, closing the legal chapter on one of the most remarkable estate sale discoveries in Arizona history. For collectors and casual shoppers alike, the case is a reminder that value is not always visible at first glance.
